extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on forming, naming, and defining general conceptions and terms so they are suitable instruments for inductive inquiry and scientific use. Covers criteria for appropriate and clear conceptions, the role of language, and principles for fixing connotation by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions must correspond to a real agreement that holds for all and only the cases of the phenomenon in question; a conception is inappropriate if it either omits some genuine cases or includes non-cases (Plurality of Causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill criticizes Aristotle's classification of spontaneous motion as inappropriate because it fails to include all spontaneous motions (e.g., planetary motion) and includes non-spontaneous cases (e.g., air rising due to water). An appropriate conception isolates the true point of agreement relevant to the purpose of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (determinateness) of conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear conception is one in which we know exactly in what the agreement consists; it is determinate, fixed, and not fluctuating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires careful observation, analysis of resemblance, and accurate memory. A person with clear ideas always knows by what properties his classes are constituted. Examples: being able to state what makes a frigate distinct from other ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and consistent application of conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once fixed, a conception should not fluctuate or be applied inconsistently; we should not class things together without knowing precisely why, nor vary the class-membership arbitrarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes to a conception should occur only consciously and for good reasons (progress of knowledge or correction of error). Avoid using general names without a precise connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational and memorial requisites for clear conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear conceptions depend on habits of attentive observation, extensive experience, and an accurate memory that retains exact images of observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The better one observes and compares a class of phenomena and the more accurate one's memory, the clearer the resulting conceptions will be. These are practical prerequisites for forming determinate concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity of faculties (scientific imagination) for finding appropriate conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance of hitting upon the appropriate conception depends on the activity and skill of the observing and comparing faculties and on the scientific imagination stored with relevant general conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mind well supplied with relevant prior conceptions and exercised in arranging known elements into new combinations is more likely to perceive the important point of agreement (e.g., recognizing planetary orbit regularities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of prematurely fixed general conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: While provisional conceptions must be formed in inquiry, premature general conceptions are impediments when they are permanently acquiesced in and prevent reclassification in light of new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We cannot frame all good conceptions beforehand; early conceptions are necessary steps but must be revisable. The danger is when a badly made class is treated as Nature-sanctioned and never corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hypotheses when direct comparison fails
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct comparison of phenomena does not reveal the important agreement, we may need to invoke previously acquired conceptions or hypotheses to guide the search for the common attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like searching for a hidden object by imagining possible hiding places, inquiry sometimes requires imaginative hypotheses derived from other knowledge to suggest where to look (e.g., using prior conceptions to find planetary orbital agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of general names for extended induction
rubrics_metrics.description: General names (and language) are practically necessary to carry out any induction beyond the simplest particulars because they serve as permanent signs that record uniformities and enable complex comparison and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without general propositions or signs, complex experimental comparison, communication of others' experience, and retention of many uniformities would be infeasible. Even brutes can make simple inductions without language, but human scientific induction requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed and knowable meaning of general names
rubrics_metrics.description: Every general name should have a meaning steadily fixed and precisely determined so that it can perform its function in induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaning resides in the connotation (the attribute(s) the name expresses). For induction, it is imperative to determine exactly the attributes a name connotes; vague or fluctuating connotations make general propositions untestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for fixing connotation of common-use names
rubrics_metrics.description: For names already in common use, the connotation is not arbitrarily chosen but must be ascertained from existing usage and associated propositions; definitions should, where possible, align with received use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose meanings that conflict with established associations and received propositions; seek to preserve the truth of generally received propositions after fixing meaning. Example: avoid defining terms so radically that accustomed true statements would become false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of defining (selection of attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a concrete name is to select, from among the many attributes common to the denoted objects, those attributes to be associated with the name—preferably attributes that are proven causes of, or sure marks for, many other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining which common properties to include often requires analysis and inductive investigation. Choose properties that serve as reliable bases for inferring other attributes and that best mark off the class for the intended theoretical or practical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition must serve a proposition or use
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is valuable only insofar as it serves some proposition or principle; the right definition is the one that helps enunciate and test the substantive claim of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical debates (e.g., uniform force, vis viva, species) are not arbitrary semantic fights but hinge on implicit propositions about nature. Always ask what principle the definition is meant to express and ensure it preserves or clarifies that principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference to preserve established propositions when redefining
rubrics_metrics.description: When fixing the meaning of an established name, prefer a connotation that does not render generally received propositions inadmissible; definitions should, as far as practicable, keep prior accepted truths intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pragmatic constraint helps ensure adoption of the new definition and continuity with prior discourse; radical redefinitions that contradict entrenched true propositions are unlikely to be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive character of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions evolve with advancing knowledge; perfect definitions are impossible until the theory of the subject is perfected, so definitions must be open to improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific progress will often suggest better connotations; accept that definitions are provisional and improve them as understanding of underlying properties and causes deepens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of names where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: A second requisite of a philosophical language is that there should be a name wherever something important needs to be designated; the language should supply names for significant concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the first requisite is steadiness of meaning, the second is availability: technical/novel names are easy to create, but common-use names require careful ascertainment of their proper connotation before fixing them.
